The United Nations. An international organization established in nineteen forty-five after World War II to maintain international peace, security, and cooperation among nations. Founded by the major Allied powers and based on the earlier League of Nations, it embodies the principle of collective security and creates a forum for diplomacy and conflict resolution. Though limited by national sovereignty and superpower rivalry, the UN has become central to international relations, peacekeeping operations, humanitarian aid, and the codification of human rights.

The organization was established by the United Nations Charter, signed on June twenty-sixth, nineteen forty-five, just after Germany's defeat, becoming effective October twenty-fourth, nineteen forty-five, after ratification by major powers. It was created in response to the League of Nations' failure to prevent World War II, incorporating lessons about requiring major powers' participation, particularly the United States, and establishing enforcement mechanisms.

The UN is organized with a General Assembly where all member nations are represented equally, a Security Council with five permanent members holding veto power, and specialized agencies for humanitarian and technical work. The five permanent Security Council members—the United States, Soviet Union, Britain, France, and China—could veto military actions, reflecting and entrenching Cold War divisions.

The organization expanded from fifty-one founding members to nearly two hundred by the late twentieth century as former colonies gained independence and joined. It has conducted peacekeeping operations in Korea, Cyprus, the Middle East, and dozens of other conflicts, with varying degrees of success. The UN became the primary institution for international legal development, including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, conventions on genocide, refugees, and the laws of war.
